Worthless means having no value, no use, or no good qualities whatsoever.

If something is worthless, it gives you nothing — no benefit, no help, no monetary value, nothing of importance. It is the complete absence of worth.

To understand it fully, start with the word "worth." Worth means the value or usefulness something has. A gold coin has worth because you can exchange it for things. A good knife has worth because it cuts. A trustworthy friend has worth because they are reliable and caring. Now add "-less" — a suffix that means "without." So worthless = without worth. Zero value. Zero usefulness.
Where the Word Applies

Worthless can describe things, people, efforts, and information. Each has its own flavour.

1. Objects and Things

When an object is worthless, it has no practical use and no monetary value.

"This cracked vase is worthless — nobody would buy it, and you can't even put water in it."

"After the company went bankrupt, its shares became worthless overnight."

A thing becomes worthless when it can no longer do what it was meant to do, or when no one finds any reason to want it.

2. People

This is the harshest use of the word. Calling a person worthless means you believe they have no good qualities, contribute nothing, and cannot be relied upon for anything.

"He was a worthless employee — he never finished a task and kept making excuses."

"Her father called her worthless, and those words stayed with her for years."

Important: Calling a person worthless is a serious insult. It is a sweeping, crushing judgment that denies them all human value. In real life, people rarely actually have zero value — this word, when applied to people, is almost always an exaggeration driven by anger or cruelty. Use it with care.

3. Efforts and Actions

An effort or action is worthless when it produces no result and leads nowhere.

"All our hard work was worthless — the entire project got cancelled."

"It's worthless arguing with him. He never listens."

Here, worthless is similar to saying the effort was pointless or futile — it achieved nothing.

4. Information, Advice, and Ideas

When information or advice is worthless, it is completely unhelpful — it does not solve your problem, it is irrelevant, or it is simply wrong.

"The map we were given was worthless — half the streets on it didn't exist."

"His advice was worthless. Following it only made things worse."
Objective vs. Subjective Worthlessness

This is an important distinction.

Objective worthlessness means something has no value by any reasonable standard — not just in your opinion, but by any measure.

A counterfeit banknote is objectively worthless as money. No store will accept it. Its "value" is an illusion.

Subjective worthlessness means you find something worthless, though others might not.

"I find reality TV completely worthless."

Here, you are expressing a personal judgment. Someone else might love reality TV and find it very valuable for entertainment.

The word can carry both meanings, so context always matters. When someone says something is worthless, ask yourself: is this a fact, or an opinion?
Feeling Worthless

The word takes on a deep emotional meaning when someone says they feel worthless.

"After losing his job and his relationship in the same month, he felt completely worthless."

To feel worthless means to feel as though you have no value as a person — that you matter to no one, that nothing you do makes a difference, that the world would be no different without you. It is one of the most painful emotional states a person can experience, and it is closely associated with depression and low self-esteem.

This use of the word is not about money or usefulness — it is about a person's sense of their own importance and place in the world.
Degrees of Worthlessness

Worthlessness is not always total. The word can be intensified or softened.

  • Completely / totally / utterly worthless — zero value, in the strongest possible terms.

    "The warranty was utterly worthless — they refused every single claim."

  • Practically worthless — almost no value, though perhaps not quite zero.

    "By the time we arrived, the medicine was practically worthless — it had expired months ago."

  • Worthless for a specific purpose — has no value in a particular context, though it might have value elsewhere.

    "A hammer is worthless for cutting wood, but perfect for driving nails."
Tone and Emotional Weight

The tone of worthless ranges from neutral to deeply hurtful, depending on what it describes.

  • Applied to objects or things: Usually neutral and factual. No emotional weight.

    "The old printer is worthless now — it doesn't support modern software."

  • Applied to efforts or information: Mildly negative. Can sound dismissive or disappointed.

    "That meeting was worthless. We decided nothing."

  • Applied to people: Very harsh and emotionally loaded. Avoid using this casually.

    "You're worthless." — This is a deeply insulting and hurtful statement.

The key rule: the more personal the target, the more emotionally destructive the word becomes.
Similar Words — and How They Differ

Understanding how worthless compares to related words will sharpen your grasp of it.

Useless — cannot perform its function. Focuses on the inability to do something.

"A pen with no ink is useless." (It can't write.)
"Useless" is often gentler than "worthless" and rarely implies total absence of value.

Valueless — has no monetary or material value. More formal and neutral.

"The land was valueless because it flooded every year."

Pointless — has no purpose or meaning. Focuses on the why, not the what.

"It's pointless to water dead plants." (There's no reason to do it.)

Futile — refers to efforts that are doomed to fail.

"It was futile to resist." (No matter what you do, it won't work.)

Good-for-nothing — applied only to people; informal and quite rude. Suggests the person is lazy and unreliable.

"He's a good-for-nothing layabout."

Meaningless — has no meaning or significance. Focuses on a lack of sense or purpose, not necessarily value.

"To him, life felt meaningless." (Not that he had no value, but that nothing seemed to matter.)

The main thing that sets worthless apart is its completeness — it suggests a total absence of value, more sweeping than most of these alternatives.
Opposite Words

If something is not worthless, it is:

  • Valuable — has significant worth or usefulness
  • Precious — of great value, often emotionally or materially
  • Priceless — so valuable it cannot be measured in money
  • Useful — can be used effectively for a purpose
  • Beneficial — produces a good result or improvement
  • Worthwhile — worth the time, effort, or cost spent on it
A Few More Examples to Cement It

"The contract was written so vaguely that it was worthless in court — it couldn't protect anyone."

"She spent three hours looking for her lost keys, and in the end the locksmith's advice was worthless — he didn't even know the model."

"Growing up in an abusive home, she was told she was worthless. It took years of therapy to unlearn that lie."

"Gold became worthless in that fictional world because everyone had too much of it."

"A parachute that doesn't open is worse than worthless — it's dangerous."
The One-Line Summary

Worthless = having absolutely no value, use, or good qualities — whether you're talking about an object, a person, an effort, or a piece of information.

The word is complete and final. It leaves nothing. Where there is worth, there is reason to care about something. Where there is worthlessness, there is not.
